tracks.title: One command, every verb
tracks.text: Last lesson — wbx. The command line. wbx is one compiled tool that authors, builds, signs, ships, and docks workbooks. The same binary on your laptop… in CI… and inside the engine. [curious] So you and your agents speak one language.

tracks.title: A bag of binaries
tracks.text: Every ecosystem eventually hands you a toolbelt. One binary to scaffold… another to build… a third to deploy… a wrapper to sign things… a daemon's client for the server bits. Each with its own flags, its own config file, its own way of being slightly out of date. [chuckles] You don't learn the tools, so much as negotiate with them. An ecosystem whose whole bet is homogeneity can't ship that. If workbooks are one artifact, and the grammar is one grammar… the tooling has to be one tool.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. wbx is the Workbooks command line. One compiled tool that authors, builds, signs, ships, and docks workbooks. The same binary on your laptop, in CI, and inside the engine. And it's deliberately thin. wbx owns almost no logic of its own. It parses what you asked… handles local org operations with the same kernel the rest of the ecosystem uses… and drives the engine for everything heavy. The intelligence lives in the system. wbx is the handle.

tracks.title: Install it
tracks.text: Installing is one line. Curl workbooks dot s h, slash c l i dot s h… piped to shell. It detects your OS and architecture. Or npm install — same thing, npm-flavored. macOS, Linux, and Windows binaries all ship from the releases. Then, let the tool check itself. Two commands. First — wbx doctor. It reports your environment and engine health… what's wired, and what isn't. And second — bare wbx, no arguments. A where-am-I landing. Version… engine state… and your likely next moves.

tracks.title: The verb families
tracks.text: Thirty-odd verbs. But they group into families — and if you learn the families, the help text carries you the rest of the way. Six of them. First: author. Init, dev, query, lint… org in, structure out. Second: make. Build and bundle — compile code to WebAssembly, tangle everything into one artifact. Third: trust. Sign and verify… provenance that travels with the file. Fourth: parts. The toolkit family — discover, build, push, import, run. Fifth: engine. Deploy, publish, workbook… stand up a Nexus, and ship to it. And sixth: the everyday verbs. Doctor… status… open… upgrade. Every family follows the same manners. [excited] And every success suggests the next verb. The tool teaches its own grammar as you go.

tracks.title: Two audiences, one binary
tracks.text: Here's the design decision that shapes everything else. wbx knows it has two kinds of users… and it changes its manners for each — without changing what it does. You, at a terminal? Human mode is deliberately dumb simple. The tool does the work. Missing argument with an obvious default? It picks the default… and tells you. Every success ends with the next verb you probably want. An agent, in a pipe? The moment stdout isn't a terminal, wbx switches. No prompts… ever. No color codes. Plain, parseable output. Add the JSON flag, and every outcome — success or failure — arrives as one envelope. A stable error code… a message… and a hint written for the agent to act on. [excited] Failures carry a stable exit-code map, so a script can branch without parsing prose. Three means the engine's unreachable — and it's retryable. Four means not found. Seven means your credentials got rejected. [chuckles] Don't retry that one blindly.

tracks.title: Your first workbook, two minutes
tracks.text: Your first workbook — two minutes, nothing assumed. You need wbx installed… that's it. No engine. No account. Step one: scaffold. wbx init, field notes. One command… one folder. Step two: see it live. wbx dev watches the org file, re-renders on every save, and serves a preview that reloads itself. Open the URL… open the org file in any editor… change a heading… save. [excited] And watch the browser follow. That loop — org file on the left, living page on the right — is the whole authoring experience. And step three: make it one file. wbx bundle tangles everything into a single, self-contained artifact. And wbx sign puts your name on it. That HTML file opens in any browser… mails like an attachment… and carries its own provenance. No server was involved at any point.

tracks.title: Import anything
tracks.text: You probably already have capability lying around. Claude skills… MCP servers… an OpenAPI spec… a little npm CLI. The intake ramp packages any of it as a toolkit. wbx toolkit import — point it at the thing, and it figures out what the thing is. Import is three honest stages… and the second two run automatically. Stage one: parse and scaffold. Docs become org, and the manifest is real. Stage two: the wasm audit. Every carried script gets classified against the sandbox lanes. Ready… convertible… or blocked. And the findings are written into the manifest — so the artifact carries its own audit. Stage three: the fix-up plan. Everything not ready becomes a to-do, with concrete steps. Which lane… which recipe… what to rewrite. [excited] It reads like a manual, because it is one. Hand the folder to an agent… and the work is already itemized. And when an engine is reachable — audit, dash dash fix. Push… build… verify. One shot.

tracks.title: Wire in an agent
tracks.text: Pointing a coding agent at wbx? Three things make it fluent immediately. First — let it discover the surface. wbx help, dash dash JSON, returns the entire verb tree as machine-readable structure. An agent never guesses at flags. Second — give it the envelope. Call everything with the JSON flag… branch on the error code and the retryable bit… instead of scraping stderr. The hint field literally names the command that fixes the problem. And third — pipe freely. Author verbs accept dash, for standard input… so generated org never needs a temp file. That's the whole integration. No SDK. No API keys for the local surface. The same binary you use… spoken plainly.

tracks.title: Same binary everywhere
tracks.text: And the part that makes wbx more than a convenience. It's one Rust crate… with two build targets. The native binary is what you install. The same source also compiles to WebAssembly — so it runs inside the engine's sandbox. Which means the agents working in a runtime container reach for the exact same tool you do. Same help text. Same manners. That's not an implementation detail… it's the trust model. When an agent's session log says wbx toolkit build, you can run the identical command and see the identical thing. [excited] No translation layer between what your crew does and what you'd do. Which is what "people and AI build together" has to mean… at the tooling level.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] What happened to w b? Renamed. The command is wbx everywhere now. If you see the old name in the wild… it's historical sediment. Do I need the engine installed? Not for the local families. Author, make, and trust work on plain files. Windows? Yes — as of oh-thirteen, it ships in every release. What's the difference between agent mode and the JSON flag? Agent mode is manners — no prompts, no color. JSON is a format — the envelope contract. Most integrations want both… [chuckles] piping gets you the first for free. And — can it really convert my Claude skill into a toolkit? It packages anything parseable, immediately. Scripts are the honest part. Shell and JavaScript usually classify ready… python is blocked until there's a lane… and everything in between gets a written fix-up plan. Rather than a shrug.

tracks.title: Wrapping up
tracks.text: And that's wbx. One command… every verb… the same binary in every hand that holds it. That's the whole tour. The file… the engine… the parts… the grammar… the crew… the gardener… and the command. [excited] Now go make something — and hand it to someone.
